utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to inform the parties that Judge Kinis, for urgent personal reasons, is unable to sit today and tomorrow. Judge Gwaunza and I have considered whether it would be interests of justice to -- to continue the hearing, and we have decided that it is in the interests of justice, and, therefore, we'll be in court, the two of us, and we'll continue to hear the case. Judge Kinis will have access to the full transcripts and, if need be, the video of -- and audio of the hearings. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, would you like me to now escort in the representatives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Monkhouse. You may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just before I begin, Mr. President, in terms of timing, if you can tell me when the break will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll -- first I would like to put on the record, which is -- has been, until now, confidential, that the Chamber had decided that we would hear the testimony of the next witness through videolink. The next witness being Mr. Mr. Akashi. Mr. Akashi, during a closed session hearing in the last half an hour, has already made a solemn declaration that he will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. As far as timing concerned, I will just consult with the registrar here for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber would like you to start your examination-in-chief and we would then take a break at 11.45, that is in five-quarters of an hour from now on. Then we would have half an hour of a break, and then we would conclude at a quarter to 2.00. Mr. Akashi, unfortunately, this morning we had a bad start because we had technical problem with the videolink which now all seem to have been resolved. They have been resolved. We'll start now with a session of five-quarters of an hour, then have half an hour break and then have a last session here in western Europe until a quarter to 2.00, and then we'll continue tomorrow, if that is fine with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's fine with me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Akashi, you will first be examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina, and Mr. Misetic are you ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could please show the witness 65 ter 1D2935 which is tab 0 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I'm going to show you now a witness statement which you signed -- or which I believe you signed and it is dated 20 July 2009. Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, have you had a chance to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I had a -- a couple of occasions when I reviewed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a statement dated 20 July 2009. On the bottom of the first page, is that a -- and on the last page, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you gave the statement to the Gotovina Defence, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After our conversation, in the last few days, I had an opportunity to consult with my notebook about my various appointments, and, on that basis, I think I must correct the information in paragraph 7. In fact, I was in Zagreb when Operation Storm occurred, and I was in Sarajevo when another military action in Sector West took place on the 1st of May. I think I was mixing these two operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, in fact, I was going to ask you, in addition to that correction, are there any other corrections at that need to be made to your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is no need for me to make other corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I asked you the same questions today in court that you were asked on the 20th of July, 2009, would you give the same answers in court today that are reflected in the statement that is in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I will give exactly the same answers, but I think essentially these are what took place and what I did. While depending on the nature of the questions now, I may give somewhat different answers to these new questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President I move to admit into evidence 65 ter 1D2935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Akashi, may I understand your last answer to be that the substance of your answers would be the same, subject to this one correction, but that, of course, it depends on the questions, whether you would give further details or -- but that the substance as it's written down is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. That's the thrust of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number to the statement of Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement will be Exhibit D1646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1646 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I'm going to turn your attention now to the events of Operation Flash in Western Slavonia, which you've referenced now in correcting your answer to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could show Mr. Akashi, please, tab 50, which is 65 ter 1D1166.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, do you recognise this document as a code cable that you sent on the 10th of May, 1995 to Mr. Annan, Mr. Gharekhan, Mr. Goulding, and Mr. Stoltenberg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not had time to read through this cable but, on the face of it, I have been present at, indeed, those meetings took place. But I -- I have not had time to review the cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, as a preliminary matter, we're going to go through many code cables today. If you could explain to the Chamber what your position was and why you were sending code cables on a frequent basis to Mr. Annan in New York?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there may be some confusion. Mr. Akashi, I think the last question that was put to you by Mr. Misetic was not whether you could, at this moment, confirm the accuracy of what is in this cable, but whether you recognise this document as a cable sent to you on its first appearance. So that is to say whether there is any reason for you to believe that what appears as a cable sent by you, whether there's any reason to believe that it would not be a cable sent by you to Mr. Kofi Annan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that simply because I have not had opportunity to read this cable since -- 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at first glance --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At first glance does it look like a cable sent by you and is there anything you -- if just going through it quickly, would there be any reason, at this moment, for you to have any doubt as to whether this is a cable sent to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks as if it was a cable, indeed, I sent to the UN Secretary-General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, again, if you could just by way of background explain your position at the time and why you were sending code cables to New York on a frequent basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, as you know, I was the Special Representative of UN Secretary-General in the former Yugoslavia, and it was my duty and my responsibility to keep the Secretary-General and the secretariat fully informed of major developments within the purview of my mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this document, the 10th of May, it refers in the first sentence to a meeting on the 9th of May, 1995, in Belgrade, first with President Milosevic and subsequently with Messrs. Martic, Mikelic, Babic, and General Celeketic. Do you recall the meeting in Belgrade on or about the 9th of May with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wonder whether I should go through the entire cable before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, just as a preliminary matter, do you recall meeting with Mr. Martic, Mikelic, Babic, and General Celeketic right after Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they -- the cable says so, so I have no reason to believe that the cable is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at the second-to-last sentence, the discussion in the cable is about your meeting and about -- with them, with the Knin leadership, and also a separate meeting with Mr. Milosevic. But in your meeting with the Knin leadership the issues concerned Sector West, which was Western Slavonia that you were discussing with them. And if you look at -- on the first page, the second-to-last sentence starts: "Milosevic is firmly of the belief that the area should be placed under the sole authority of the United Nations, and every effort made to allow the Serbs from that area to continue to live there; Martic, however, maintains his position that the United Nations should do everything it can to facilitate the departure of any remaining Serbs." Now, do you have an independent recollection of Mr. Martic and the Knin leadership, after Operation Flash, taking the position that the United Nations needed to facilitate the departure of any Serbs remaining in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a specific recollection on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you could turn to page 4 of the document, which is paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your witness statement that you gave to the Gotovina Defence at paragraph 2, you stated that you recalled Operation Safe Passage and that that was to ensure maximum safety and security of innocent civilians. And let me now show you some more specifics about this meeting with the Knin leadership. Again paragraph 7 says you met for three-hours with so-called President Martic, Mikelic, Babic, and Celeketic. If we turn to paragraph 8, the first sentence says: "On Sector West I explained at length the efforts of UNCRO and other international organisations to address the explicit concerns conveyed to us by the Knin leadership, my conviction that the Serbs remaining were being well looked after, and that the programme of departure for those Serbs wishing to leave was scheduled to begin that day." Now, if we stop right there, do you recall what you meant when you stated to Mr. -- to the Knin leadership that it was your conviction that the Serbs remaining in Sector West were being well looked after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a specific recollection on this point, but I must have had the -- a general context of our continuing discussion with the leadership of the Croatian government, including Mr. Sarinic. They gave us -- they continued to give us assurances about the safety of the Serbs in Sector West, and so I must have based my belief in that regard on these conversations I had -- I was having in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you go down in that paragraph towards the middle, at the sentence that begins "after rather extensive discussions ..." Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which -- what line?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's in the middle of paragraph 8, and it begins: "After rather extensive discussions Martic asked me four questions ..." "After rather extensive discussions, Martic asked me" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now I found the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Martic asked me four questions: 1, how long will it take to move all the Serbs from Sector West to Serb-controlled Bosnia." Do you remember Mr. Martic asking you that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection about this particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you go down a few lines it says -- you write what you responded. And you said: "I responded that, 1, I could give no time assurances, the important consideration being that the people's right to choose was being respected." Now, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid that I have no recollection of these specific points discussed between Martic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President I move to admit 65 ter 1D1166 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit D1647.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1647 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could go -- just one moment, please. If we could go to 65 ter 1D1176. This is tab 1, Mr. Registrar, in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There concerns a meeting with Milan Babic. And if we -- if you go to the second page, Mr. Akashi, that's the page that I'm interested in. It's from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Kirudja to you. Can you tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, first, if you look at the memorandum heading on page 2 of the document. It's to you from Mr. Kirudja. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the first page of this document should be to Stoltenberg from Colborne; is that correct? If I could get the assistance of Mr. Registrar in Tokyo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I think we've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It's on the second page, two of five?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we scroll up in e-court, it's 2 of 5 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, again, could you tell the Court who Mr. Kirudja was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not know who Mr. Kirudja is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's a memo that was sent to you on the 10th of May discussing a meeting with Mr. Milan Babic, a proposal for Western Slavonia. And if we go to paragraph 2, this is now -- purports to be the words of Mr. Babic. The sentence at the bottom of the stage starts: "We are all interested in the fate of the people in Western Slavonia, and we know that the majority want to leave and" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... not remain under Croatian authority. We also know that the Croats have intensified their propaganda campaign to show to everybody that they are ... humane -- that they are a humane occupying force of our lands." Now, the first question, Mr. Akashi, is: Since you don't recall who Mr. Kirudja was, I presume you don't recall this memo specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is it, your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving a memo like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I do not have a specific recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of this cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As -- as a general matter - let me ask you the more general question. As a general matter what information were you receiving from the Knin leadership about the desire of the Serb population in Western Slavonia after Operation Flash, in terms of whether they wished to stay or leave Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general, we received information about Krajina Serb leadership from our own representatives who are stationed in Knin, including commander of UN peacekeeping force there. And on the civilian side, I remember that we had a very able representative called Jack Greenberg who kept us all [indiscernible] about Knin's Serb leadership's behaviour, and, to the extent possible, their thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you remember specifically now what the thinking of the Knin Serb leadership was on the issue of whether Serbs should stay or leave Western Slavonia after Operation Flash took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have specific recollection as to which course of action Knin Serb leadership was in favour of: Departure or staying on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I move to admit into evidence 65 ter 1D1176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, no objections, I understand. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit D1648.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar in Tokyo, the next document will be tab 2 in the binder, and this is 65 ter 1D1177.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, this is a memo --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll wait for it come up on the screen here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a memo drafted by you and sent to Mr. Annan on the 9th of May, 1995, and talks about the movement of Serbs from Pakrac. Pakrac is in Western Slavonia. And in the first paragraph you write: "Today marked the successful start of the operation to relocate willing, informed Serbs from Sector West to Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then you discuss what procedures were employed. It says: "This morning approximately 300 Serbs gathered in Pakrac in response to the UNHCR notification by radio of the possibility of departing from Sector West. Each individual was interviewed by the Croatian authorities with respect to their civil rights and then interviewed/counselled by the UNHCR on their right to remain if they so wished. If after this point individual Serbs still wished to department, their names were taken by UNPF staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page and go to paragraph 7 it says: "Other villages" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says : "Other villages/towns are now being examined and a consolidated list of dates for each location will be broadcast by radio to the local population." And the preceding paragraph discusses the planning of subsequent movements, including when the convoys would be leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, first, do you have -- does this refresh your recollection about some of the specifics of Operation Safe Passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not have recollection about these specific points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have a recollection that the United Nations was involved in transferring Serbs out of Western Slavonia and into Bosnia and Herzegovina after Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not recall these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President I move to admit 65 ter 1D1177, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1649.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1649 is admitted into evidence. I take that if I do not hear from the other Defence teams that there are no objections against the documents tendered by Mr. Misetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar in Tokyo, tab 3 is the next document. And Mr. Registrar here in The Hague, it's 65 ter 1D2915. And I have to -- I'm reminded that I need to seek leave to add this to our 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, any objections to the document being added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me just look at it. I suspect there are none but I'll -- give me a few seconds. Yeah, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add this document to the 65 ter list. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, this is a report of -- from UNHCR on humanitarian issues that was sent to the ICFY co-chairman on the 30th of June, and it discusses Operation Safe Passage. And if we could go to page 4 of the document in e-court, and it's numbered page -- numbered page 3, Mr. Akashi, at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's numbered page 3, and I'm interested now in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- in the paragraph that begins in the middle of the page: "The influx of refugees from Western Slavonia ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And towards the end of that paragraph, there's a statistic and it says: "Some 2.100 left Western Slavonia ... via the UNCRO Operation Safe Passage?" And then the next paragraph says: "The Croatian government" -- in the middle of the paragraph. "The Croatian government declared that those Serbs who fled Western Slavonia will be permitted to return if it is ascertained that they were legally residents in Croatia prior to the 1991 conflict. UNHCR's involvement in the population movements from Western Slavonia after the restoration of Croatian rule was limited to the counselling of the Serb population about their right to stay or the possibility to leave with the assistance of international organisations. In the latter case, UNHCR ascertained the voluntary nature of such departures. The UNHCR also interviewed refugees arriving from Sector West to Banja Luka." Mr. Akashi, in terms of the departure of the Serb population from Western Slavonia and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well ... yes. Please answer the question. We had to wait, Mr. Akashi, for a while for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- Mr. Akashi, I will complete the question. In terms of the departure of the -- the organised departure of the Serbs from Western Slavonia through international organisations, do you have a recollection as to whether it was ever established whether those departures were voluntary or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was a standard policy of UNHCR to ascertain the voluntary nature of movement of the people concerned. Otherwise, it would constitute a forceful departure. So what is mentioned in this paragraph looks to me to represent the standing UNHCR policy in these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As part of determining the voluntariness of the departure, do you know if UNHCR asked Serbs who wished to depart, whether they would sign a document indicating the voluntariness of the departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the technicality of how the voluntary nature of these refugee departure was ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to admit 65 ter 1D295 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1650.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1650 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me call up one document, which I may not have any questions for in light of the last answer. But, nevertheless, it's 65 ter 1D2914. And it's page 2, paragraphs 8 and 9, Mr. President, go to the issue of the procedures employed by UNHCR to determine voluntariness, and I will move across the bar table do admit this one into evidence as well, and I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could just have until the break so can I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be marked for identification for the time being. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D1651 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I wish to turn your attention now to the events leading up to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, first of all, attending a meeting with President Tudjman on or about the 29th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a specific recollection of that meeting on the 29th of July with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, fortunately we had an audio recording of the meeting, so I would like to play for you some excerpts of the audio of your meeting with President Tudjman on the 29th of July, 1995. It may refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, this is 65 ter 1D1166. And if I may just have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the top of the audio clip --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave -- called out the wrong number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was 65 ter 1D2943, if that's the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was provided with a copy in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the issue is that in the meeting President Tudjman has his own interpreter present who is conducting an interpretation, so the question for the Chamber is whether you wish for the interpreters in the booths to be interpreting the Croatian followed by President Tudjman's interpreter or should we just let the audio play as is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think for a better understanding it is important to know how the language spoken by Mr. Akashi was translated to President Tudjman and how the words of Mr. Tudjman were translated to Mr. Akashi, and, therefore, exceptionally, I think that it would be appropriate to -- well not to say to rely upon, but at least to follow the conversation as it was translated at the time. Which, of course, then creates an additional problem in relation to the French translation. It's -- it's the first time that I'm thinking about these problems, because what we then expect from the French translators to first translate what is said in English and then to translate the words as translated in B/C/S. It's a bit of a puzzle. I suggest to the parties that we invite the French booth -- I always am -- don't know exactly the -- oh, the other side, yes, to translate on the basis of the transcript but only to translate the words as spoken by the person himself; that is, for Mr. Akashi, English, and for President Tudjman, the words in B/C/S. I hope that that will work. If have you any problems with that, I'd like to know. I'll move to channel 5 to hear any. Then we'll proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are starting at the 26th minute, 59 second mark of the tape. And this is page 9 of the transcripts for the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, we're going to begin now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Shall we continue from where we are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think what will now follow is the translation by the interpreter as given at the time. So I think we still can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Mr. President said: We don't -- I don't think we need fear such as human tragedies because as we can see the Serbs are demoralised, deserting their units. So either they will show their readiness to agree to a political solution or they will be -- they will suffer a military defeat. And speaking quite openly, I think both the European Community, the European Union, and the United Nations are quite aware of the Serbian behaviour, and have shown full understanding of the steps Croatia has taken in this regard. "So let me repeat: We are for talks, for negotiations, if the peace process should start right away, not in eight days or in a fortnight but in two or three days, but the peace process must start right away. Otherwise, we shall take advantage of the demoralisation in the Serbian ranks both in Bosnia and among the Knin Serbs. "Therefore, it is not at all fortuitous that Martic, Karadzic, and Mladic have been proclaimed criminals of war, and this I believe that also reflects the general mood, the general position of the international community, and I think the other side should draw its conclusions from that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I may not have understood the previous guidance of the Court. I thought that everything would be translated to make sure -- to understand what was actually spoken by President Tudjman and what was said by the interpreter. I did not get an English interpretation of what President Tudjman directly said. I'm not saying that we need it, but I thought is how it was going to proceed. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said that exceptionally we would focus on how it was translated at the time and, of course, if there's any need to verify the translation, we have, of course, now the transcript in both languages so there is an opportunity to verify that, if there's any need to do so. At the same time, I'm not quite convinced yet that the B/C/S transcript, as you find it on our screen, is exactly the same as the B/C/S transcript as we -- I mean, on the e-court screen, is exactly the same as the transcript we find in the transcribed version of this conversation as far as B/C/S is concerned. But there's an opportunity to verify that, because it's all written, and most important, at this moment for Mr. Akashi seems to be how his language was translated to President Tudjman at the time, the words he used, and how the language of Mr. Tudjman was translated to him. This gives, I take it, a better orientation. Unless the parties would come with strong reasons to follow another procedure. Then you may proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Yasushi Akashi: Mr. President, if you agree, I'd be ready to fly to Knin tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, and to convey your willingness to start serious political talks. "The Interpreter: The president said: If this should lead to a peaceful solution and this means that we should have the immediate reinstatement of the pipeline, meaning within 24 hours, and immediate start of the negotiations of reinstatement of road and rail links, but immediately. "Including also political talks on the implementation of the constitutional law of the Republic of Croatia on the rights of the Serbian ethnic community in Croatia, the rights to local self-government ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, did you follow along with the audio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very well. I missed some -- some -- some of the passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you recall you having a discussion with President Tudjman about going to Knin and President Tudjman giving you some of his conditions that the Knin leadership needed to accept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I remember that I met President Tudjman on the 29th of July, and the atmosphere at the time was extremely grave and with some forebodings of a major war starting, and I remember also that I made my best effort to counsel self-restraint to President Tudjman. Other than that, specifics escape my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move for the admission of the audio of that meeting, which is, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 1D2943. We don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D1652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, you ultimately did go to Knin and have that meeting with Mr. Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Registrar, in Tokyo, if you could show Mr. Akashi the document in tab 5. And, Mr. Registrar, here this is 65 ter 1D1586.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, this is the code cable you sent to Mr. Annan documenting what transpired at that meeting with Mr. Martic on 30th of July in Knin. And I'd like to spend a few minutes talking to you about this meeting. Now, in paragraph 1 you describe the document in front of you as a comprehensive summary of that meeting. And in paragraph 2 you write: "I went to Knin with the intention of exacting very specific commitments from the leadership there on measures to be taken that would clearly contribute a stabilisation of the situation." And towards the middle of that paragraph, you note that the meeting lasted for over five and one-half hours. If you turn the page and go to paragraph 3. You describe what commitments you sought from the Knin leadership, and you identify four commitments that you ask them to make. And then the last sentence of paragraph 3 says: "In return for these commitments, I was prepared to order an active deployment of UNCRO forces along the likely main axis of any potential HV advance into the Krajina, provided that the necessary security and freedom of movement' assurances for UNCRO troops were provided by the ARSK, and to dedicate all my efforts of persuasion at convincing the Croatian authorities to pursue negotiations rather than war." Now can you explain what was the intention -- had the Knin leadership accepted these four points, what was "the active deployment of UNCRO forces along the likely main axis of any potential advance into the Krajina ..." intended to do by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, what is your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it indicates that you made -- that you were prepared to order active deployment of UNCRO forces along the likely main axis of any potential HV advance in the Krajina. My question is: Why? What would the deployment of the UNCRO forces along the main axis of any potential HV advance have achieved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a recollection as to my thinking when these discussions actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any concern that deploying UNCRO forces along a likely main axis of any potential HV advance might put those forces, those UNCRO forces, in harm's way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot answer that question, because whatever I say will be based on a supposition of mine today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 10 of this document, which is numbered page 4. And it's page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 states: "The Force Commander" -- who I believe was General Janvier at this meeting, "supported my efforts throughout the meeting, and by making the following explicit points to Martic and Mrksic: ... there was a need for precise, concrete commitments from the RSK to avoid a military escalation." And then the fourth point was: "NATO close air support is available for him to use against any force attacking United Nations personnel." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If -- let me ask you this question: Based on your experience in the former Yugoslavia, if UNCRO was deployed along the likely main axis of attack by the HV, based on your understanding of this entry, would NATO have been called in had there been an altercation then between the HV and UNCRO forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question -- Mr. Akashi, before you answer the question, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two points. First of all, that, I think, calls for clear speculation, especially given the witness's recollection so far to that meeting. Second of all, there are four points, so if Mr. Misetic will call for speculation, rather than read two of them at least the whole -- the whole paragraph, all four points, should be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you're invited to give the full context and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you further asked the witness about based on your understanding of this entry, where, of course, we would have to know what the understanding of the witness of this entry is before we can fully evaluate this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if could I ask just -- just to give a proffer of what's -- what I'm going to do. If I could ask that the -- is there any way for the witness not to listen to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any way that you could postpone that for a couple of minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- just before the break hear from you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me read out the full paragraph for you, Mr. Akashi. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I had read out: "The Force Commander supported my efforts throughout the meeting and by making the following explicit points to Martic and Mrksic: (a), there was a need for precise concrete commitments from the RSK to avoid a military escalation; (b), Croatia considers the ARSK involvement in Bihac as justification for its own military moves in Grahovo and Glamoc; (c), the RSK cannot complain about the United Nations's inability to implement our mandate if it does not provide us with the minimum degree of freedom of movement needed for us operate; and (d), NATO close air support is available for him to use against any force attacking United Nations personnel." Now my question to you, Mr. Akashi, is: UNCRO actually - and we can look at the document if necessary - did implement something called operation active presence, which is Exhibit D288 in this case, deploying UN forces along the main axis of potential attack by the HV. My question to you is: Did NATO, or did you and Mr. Janvier have the authority then to call in NATO to attack Croatian forces if in fact those UN forces came under fire by Croatian troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This specific NATO action is called close air support. It's an action by NATO when UN personnel is under armed attack, and the object of NATO air action will be specifically the weapon which is used actually against the safety and the security of UN personnel. And the weapons attacking UN personnel have to be verified, not only from the air but from the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do not mind, I'd like to intervene for a second. I think the specific question by Mr. Misetic was whether you or Mr. Janvier had the authority to call for such a NATO close air support. So the question is less about what that means but, rather, about who had the authority to call for such an action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case, there's a standard procedure called dual-key system. In other words, activation of NATO air action has to have not only the UN key but NATO key, in order to be implemented. So NATO can use its veto, even if -- even if UN wants it. But I was also describing specific circumstances in which UN will ask for NATO close air support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, in view of the tapes, which are not serving us for many more minutes, I suggest that we already allow Mr. Akashi to start his break and that you address the Chamber without Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- being able to hear it. Mr. Akashi, a little bit earlier than expected --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll have a break and we'd like to resume in 35 minutes from now, if that suits you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, but I take it that the break is not just form me but for all the personnel involved in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're perfectly right, but the Chamber was informed that you may have some concerns about breaks and timing, whereas all those involved in the proceedings here they know me well enough that I will consider their interests to the extent possible. But I specifically addressed you in this respect. We'd like to see you back and we can interrupt at least the audio at this moment with Tokyo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your humanitarian consideration. But I stood up to many hours of negotiations in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then we'll interrupt at least the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The point of the question is based on the fact that on 4th of August I have a code cable from Mr. Akashi indicating that on the day of Operation Storm he had a meeting with Mr. Sarinic and indicated that NATO close air support was possible because of attacks on Croatian Army troops. So I think he should have, anyway, at least some knowledge of the -- of the situation concerning NATO close air support and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, I interrupted him, I think specifically on the point you're raising now, whether the circumstances to call for close air support by NATO were met yes or no. It was not your question. Your question was about authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I want to resume that at any later stage, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course. Now, Mr. Hedaraly, do you still have any concerns about the context, as you said, and whether or not to ask for speculation. I think the witness started answering about conditions under which NATO CAS would be possible, and he apparently has knowledge about the authority to call for such air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, you are correct, and perhaps rather than showing him first that specific line, if -- in direct examination it may have been more useful to explore that with the witness, first, what his knowledge is, and then it would have obviated any contextual or speculation objection because then we would have known what the witness's knowledge was on that issue and then Mr. Misetic could have explored that further. And if then there was need to show him a specific document or cable, because either it's a contradiction or to refresh his memory, I think that then there would be no objection whatsoever. But I'm happy to wait for Mr. Misetic to resume and how the question will be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, a general invitation to be less leading through documents, and I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not affirm further support for the objection Mr. Hedaraly made before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will state that given the witness's ability to recall things independently which I have personal knowledge having tried to take a statement from him, and I think matters have proceeded very slowly this morning on that basis, I can proceed that way of testing his memory and then showing him documents, but I can assure the court that we will be in direct examination into Thursday if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps even a short introductory question, it would appear that the witness has no specific recollection about certain events, then we could move quickly then to the documents. We will take the break now, and we'll resumed at quarter past 12.00, European time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Hedaraly, D1651.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that also include that would you not object to having it added to the 65 ter list, if Mr. Misetic would have asked you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If he would have asked me, I would not have objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then leave is granted to add D1651 to the 65 ter list and it is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Had I asked Mr. Hedaraly and he not objected, I would have thanked him for not objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, if I could ask to you look at the document at tab 5 where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "I then tried to pin Martic down on the commitments that I believed he had made during the course of our discussion. I observed that Martic had committed himself to the following ... And it goes through: "(a), ensuring there was no ARSK presence in Bihac, which was the tantamount to an immediate and total ARSK withdrawal from Bihac; (b), that the RSK had no territorial or offensive military intentions toward Bihac; (c), that UNHCR aid deliveries to Bihac would not be hindered by the RSK authorities; and (d), that army commanders should meet right away as early as tomorrow." And if we skip down to paragraph 13, It says: "In the end, agreement was finally reached on the exact wording of the text with the understanding that Martic would sign it. As it was evident that the meeting was concluding, Mr. Matsura, who was with the ARSK, asked me if I had asked President Tudjman to sign a similar document. The answer to that question was, of course, well known to all present, and there had been no mention of the issue at any other time during the meeting. Nonetheless, Martic used it as an excuse not to sign the document. As an alternative, it was agreed that Mr. Matsura, as a fluent English speaker, would read the document out verbatim and in the name of President Martic to the waiting press. I expressed my conviction that by doing so Martic was fully accepting on his honour the terms of the commitments contained in the document. However, when we went down to meet the press, Matsura was the only one from the delegation not to accompany us (except General Mrksic who had left the meeting as soon as final agreement on the text was reached)." Now, Mr. Akashi, what conclusion did you reach by the fact that Mr. Martic refused to sign it and then Mr. Matsura did not come down to read the statement verbatim, as had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that this was with one of the ipsos of great difficulty of negotiating with Martic, and either he changed his mind or he was not -- he did not think through while we were negotiating, and he had a second mind. In the end, I think it was extremely disagreeable for us to negotiate with such a person, and we were all very bitter at the end of that meeting, which, in the end, proved to be fruitless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could look just at -- you will see that attached to this document which you sent to Mr. Annan. If you look at the last page, it is a copy of the six-point document, which, at paragraph 15 the code cable you say you are attaching for ease of reference. Another copy of the six-point document that resulted from my meeting in Knin."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you see the six-point document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D1586 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D1653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1653 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar in Tokyo, if we could please go to tab 9 in the binder. And, Mr. Registrar, this is Exhibit D1474 for e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, you will see that this is a letter you wrote to President Tudjman about your meeting in Knin with Mr. Martic. And in the cover letter, you wrote: "During discussions today in Knin, Mr. Martic reiterated to myself and General Janvier the commitment of the Knin leadership to a peaceful solution of the conflict. Six specific undertakings were also made. The exact wording of the undertakings made to me by the Knin leadership is recorded on the attached document, which I distributed to the media on my return to this evening to Zagreb." And if we turn to the page, it's the same six-point agreement that was attached to your code cable to Mr. Annan. And my question to you is, if, as you say you were -- I don't have the transcript in front of me, Mr. President, because my transcript has gone down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed that this is a problem which occurs in all the courtrooms at this moment. So, therefore, I am afraid that we have either to live with it and find solutions or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will then try to paraphrase your answer to the last document, Mr. Akashi. If you were disappointed by the fact that Mr. Martic had in fact not agreed to the six-point agreement, may I ask why you then followed up by writing a letter to President Tudjman which seems to indicate that he did accept it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should read carefully this covering letter, in which Martic reiterated his commitment to us to a peaceful solution of the conflict. He also, at one stage, agreed to the six-point undertakings, but he subsequently backtracked on that. So you can see from this covering letter differentiation between Martic's general commitment to a peaceful solution of the conflict and his acceptance of the six points in -- contained in the attached document, where I did not say that there has been agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So a careful distinction is being made between one general commitment and the six specific undertakings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask a few more questions on this topic because it relates, for us, to the Brioni transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if I may follow up. Mr. Akashi, the wording actually of the letter says simply: "I agree with you on the first sentence." The seconds sentence says: "Six specific undertakings were also made. The exact wording of the undertakings made to me by the Knin leadership is recorded on the attached document." Now, do you recognize that the wording of this letter would have indicated to President Tudjman that, in fact, Mr. Martic had agreed to these six conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His agreement with us at one point is a matter of historical record, and in order to show that the Knin leadership accepted these six undertakings at some point, we differentiated the general commitment from the historical fact of the acceptance of those undertakings at some point. Maybe this is too fine a point for a casual reader, but I think this is a carefully crafted document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that -- I'm sorry it's already admitted into evidence as D1474.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, if we could now turn to Mr. -- or to President Tudjman's response to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D1475. And it is tab 10, it's the next tab in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- first, let me know when you've had a chance to read through the letter, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not able to read Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the registrar in Tokyo could assist us. Is there an English translation of this document in the binder?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] There doesn't appear to be an English translation immediately behind the B/C/S original, so I'm looking for that elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It may that be there's inadvertently the Croatian version was put in rather than the English. So let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, ask you about your recollection. Do you recall that President Tudjman wrote you a letter in response to your letter to him of the 29th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the 28th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember Tudjman's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to tab 8 in the binder. This is 65 ter 1D1585.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, this is a code cable concerning your meeting with Mr. Sarinic on the 4th of August, which is the first day of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, towards the middle, it says -- I'll refer you to Mr. Sarinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "He expressed full understanding for the need to avoid as much as possible civilian casualties and assured me that firm orders had been passed throughout the chain of command that the security of UN personnel was to be fully respected?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Sarinic also gave official endorsement to the idea that, in the event that the Croatian Army takes long swaths of territory, the United Nations would be permitted to monitor human rights and assist on humanitarian matters."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then skipping that next sentence: "In response to my comment on the possibility of NATO close air support as to protect our troops if they are under fire, Sarinic said that NATO action in Croatia against Croatia would severely harm the relations between his government and the United Nations." And it says: "Below is a more complete summary of the meeting."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes, Mr. Misetic, someone is listening to keep the right pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying myself, Mr. President. If we could go to page 2 of this document. In that carry-over paragraph from the previous page, towards the middle, it says: "I expressed my regret that more than 200 shells had fallen on the town of Knin, that other towns in the Krajina had been shelled, that many of UNCRO's observation posts ... had been targeted, attacked, and/or overrun, that one Danish peace keeper had been killed by direct fire from the Croatian Army, and that two Polish peacekeepers were injured, one of them seriously. Although the ARSK had also shelled some Croatian cities today, such activity was subsequent to the Croatian shelling of Knin and in any case, I insisted it was not a justifiable pretext for shelling urban areas. I informed Sarinic that, after consultations with me, the Force Commander had asked NATO for air presence in areas where UNCRO peacekeepers were under direct threat from the fighting, and urged Sarinic to ensure that the HV commanders were fully cognizant of the United Nations's intention to take all necessary measures to protect its forces." Now, on this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, do you recall this discussion with Mr. Sarinic on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, yeah, some recollection about the general tone of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now you make reference in the code cable to having had a -- consultations with the Force Commander, who was General Janvier asking for NATO air presence? Do you recall the conversation with General Janvier on NATO air presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the contents of our discussion, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that NATO air presence had been called in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no specific recollection. We had occasions about possible NATO action, but I do not recall specific discussion between myself and General Janvier in this particular circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, rather than flipping back and fourth between document, Mr. President, I'm just going to read out a portion of Exhibit D288 which is General Janvier's order for active presence. It's page 6 of that order, which is also, if necessary, tab 6 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, General Janvier, prior to Operation Storm, had ordered an operation known as Active Presence, and he had ordered upon renewed hostilities UNCRO forces shall remain in location; upon renewed hostilities, all actions necessary for self-defence shall be taken; UNCRO forces shall not withdraw nor shall positions be abandoned without authorisation. And earlier in that order, General Janvier had ordered - this is page 3 of 8 at the top - within the Zone of Separation and the Dinara mountains, UNCRO forces are to be placed in those areas most likely to become either areas of conflict between the warring parties or axes of advance. My question for you, Mr. Akashi, is was there a discussion about deploying UNCRO forces in areas likely to be the main axis of attack of the HV for the purpose of ultimately calling in NATO close air support in order to stop the -- any potential Croatian Army offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give a specific answer as to whether there were specific discussions about these questions of UNCRO deployment and NATO air cover for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you say you can't -- you don't recall specific discussions. Do you recall generally any such policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection, but I think, under the circumstances, consideration might have been given to this type of measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can go back to tab 8, which is the 4th of August code cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, again, it was 1D1585. Going to page 3, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 says: "On the subject of civilians, Sarinic claimed that Croatia would like all the people to remain in the Krajina after the operation is over, as it had wished the people to stay in Western Slavonia, and that the human rights of those remain would be guaranteed. Sarinic stated that he accepted UNPF monitoring of the behaviour of Croatian military, police, and civilian authorities" -- I believe it should say "in the field of human rights and humanitarian assistance in the future in areas of the Krajina taken by the HV. He officially accepted my proposal to deploy at least two integrated human rights monitoring teams to each of Sector North and Sector South when conditions would permit. Sarinic also pledged that the entire leadership, from the top to the bottom, would do its best to behave in an civilised manner and assured me that efforts were being made to avoid civilian casualties." Now, Mr. Akashi, my first question to you is: When Mr. Sarinic told you this, did you believe that he was sincere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether I believed he was sincere?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This question can only be answered in the context of my press conference statement that day, in which I condemned the Croatian military attack on the Krajinas. And in my subsequent meeting with Sarinic in person I expressed deep regret, and I sought assurance for full safety for civilians as well as for UN personnel and additional assurances for full protection of human rights after the military action was over. So -- and I call your attention to a few words which you did not read out after the sentence which you just read for the benefit of the -- of the Tribunal, that -- that Sarinic added to say that, and I quote: "War is a terrible environment and it is the civilians who always suffer the most in such conditions." He was obviously not perhaps contrite but on the defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at paragraph 7, which offers some of your conclusions from the meeting. And you wrote: "Generally speaking, Sarinic appeared to be greatly concerned that events would transpire on the ground which would show Croatia in an unfavorable light. Because of these concerns, I believe we can expect generally good cooperation from the Croatian authorities in the areas of our own greatest concern now, namely, assistance to the civilian population and security for United Nations personnel. Although the cooperation will be welcome, to the extent it materialises, it will be the result of Croatian self-interest interest, rather than munificence. Nonetheless, Croatian anxiety over their image in the eyes of the world can be used in an appropriate manner to advance our concerns." Now, can you explain to the Court what you meant in that in terms of advancing your concerns and how Croatian anxiety could be used to advance those concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this passage requires no explanation. As I have said, our concerns were genuine and serious, and Sarinic, in his rather vain manner, did his best to -- to show his agreement with our concerns. But we were counting on -- on those Croatian interests to maintain its good image in the western countries, because we may be accused of being too optimistic in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, there is an agreement here that is referred to often in this case as the Akashi-Sarinic agreement to the 6th of August. To the best of your recollection, did the negotiations for that agreement first begin with this conversation with Mr. Sarinic on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. It perhaps may make more sense to first ask him about the agreement, what he remembers about it, and then perhaps where it started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, that's -- Mr. Hedaraly is not very strong in his expression that he would like you to be less leading, but that's certainly what he seeks, and he does it in a gentle way by not firmly objecting but by inviting you to be less leading in this respect. If you would follow his invitation, that might save us a few objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, do you recall agreement that you reached with Mr. Sarinic on the issue of human rights in the newly liberated territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the agreement on the 6th of August, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a general recollection that the agreement dealt essentially with human rights and the right of safe page for Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was the first time -- the first negotiation with Mr. Sarinic that culminated on the agreement of the 6th, the meeting on the 4th of August that is memorialised in this code cable of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In other words, this agreement on 6th of August, when was the first time had you a conversation with Mr. Sarinic about human rights monitoring by UNPF in the newly liberated territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had discussions on these matters in May, with regard to Sector West, and I -- I remember that we also discussed these matters on the 4th, 5th, and the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that Exhibit 65 ter 1D1585 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1654.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1654 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if could I have the witness look at tab 63 in the binder, which is 65 ter 1D1596, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, do you recall information regarding the shelling of Knin being given to you on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the Croatian attack on Knin started that day, I'm sure all the information about the extent and the variety of attacks should have been given to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You are not in the heading of the memo, but if we scroll down to the bottom of the page, if you look it says: "Internal distribution," and the first letters there are SRSG. Would that be you, Special Representative for the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you go -- if we look back up at the top and look at the time stamps on this document, it says UNPROFOR communications, 4 August, 8.15. And then there is a time stamp on the right-hand side of the document which appears to show a time stamp of 8.41 on the 4th of August, 1995. Now, Mr. Akashi, this is within three hours, three and a half hours, of the Croatian military operation beginning. And if you look at paragraph 2, the information distributed says: "At 0500 hours 4 August the HV commenced a coordinated and concentrated artillery attack on Knin. Over a period of 30 minutes, it is estimated that 200 to 300 rounds landed in the centre of the city. At 0530 hours, the concentrated artillery attack subsided, however, harassment fire has continued, with approximately one round every 15 seconds landing in the city centre?" First, do you recall this as the initial information that you received about the shelling of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it corresponds to my general recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence, which is 65 ter 1D1596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no objection by Mr. Hedaraly, I see. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1655 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, let me go back in time for one moment and this is tab 57 in your binder, which is 65 ter 1D1587. Again, this is a code cable from you to Mr. Annan. And if we go to page 2, paragraph 4(B). It says: "The Croatian government is not prepared to liberate all the occupied territory in the near-term offensive. They appear unprepared to take back parts of Sectors North and South and are unlikely to attack Sector East. Thus, the action would not shed the political weight of refugees from Vukovar." Now, in the days leading up to Operation Storm do you recall whether the assessment was that the Croatian Army would not conduct an operation against all of Sectors North and South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Hedaraly. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1656.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1656 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next document is Exhibit D337. And, Mr. Registrar, this is tab 11 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, this is a code cable drafted by you on the evening of the 4th of August. The UNPROFOR communications stamp in the upper right-hand corner has a time stamp of 1947. And it's an update on the current situation in Croatia, and this is the first day of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page and go to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You wrote to Mr. Annan: "We have been advised by the civil affairs office in Sector South that the Knin leadership have requested UNHCR and UNPF assistance in evacuating approximately 32.000 civilians from Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, and Knin to Petrovac and Banja Luka in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now do you recall, on the evening of the 4th, the issue of Krajina Serbs leaving the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have specific recollection of that. By the way, you said I drafted this cable. I -- these cables are usually drafted by my colleagues, either in the civilian sector, or sometimes in the military areas, and it is very occasional that I myself draft something which would be rather of general character on strategic questions than on tactical situations or specifics of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us who, by name, would have participated in drafting these cables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had seven or eight officials working for me. In addition, I had my military commander and his staff, and we had also representatives deployed in various duty stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it is impossible to tell you as to who in specific circumstances may have drafted or has sent drafts of various cables.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, would Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
